prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

On the birthday of the world I begin to contemplate what I have done and left undone, but this year not so much rebuilding of my perennially damaged psyche, shoring up eroding friendships, digging out stumps of old resentments that refuse to rot on their own. No, this year I want to call myself to task for what I have done and not done for peace. How much have I dared in opposition? How much have I put on the line for freedom? For mine and others? As these freedoms are pared, sliced and diced, where have I spoken out? Who have I tried to move? In this holy season, I stand self-convicted of sloth in a time when lies choke the mind and rhetoric bends reason to slithering choking pythons. Here I stand before the gates opening, the fire dazzling my eyes, and as I approach what judges me, I judge myself. Give me weapons of minute destruction. Let my words turn into sparks.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: How, For, Who

outputs.L1:
On the birthday of the world, I begin to contemplate what I have done and what I have left undone. Yet this year, my thoughts turn less to the rebuilding of my perennially damaged psyche, the shoring up of eroding friendships, or the digging out of the stumps of old resentments that refuse to rot on their own. No, this year I want to call myself to account for what I have done—and failed to do—for peace.

How much have I dared in opposition? How much have I put on the line for freedom—my own and that of others? As these freedoms are pared, sliced, and diced, where have I spoken out? Whom have I tried to move?

In this holy season, I stand self-convicted of sloth in a time when lies choke the mind and rhetoric bends reason into slithering, suffocating pythons. Here I stand before the opening gates, the fire dazzling my eyes; and as I approach what judges me, I judge myself.

Give me weapons of minute destruction. Let my words turn into sparks.
outputs.L2: On the world’s birthday, I start to take stock of what I have accomplished and what I have neglected. Yet this year, my thoughts are less on repairing my endlessly wounded spirit, reinforcing friendships worn thin, or uprooting the old grudges that will not decay by themselves. This year, instead, I want to hold myself accountable for what I have and have not done in the service of peace. How boldly have I resisted? What have I risked for liberty—my own and everyone else’s? As those liberties are trimmed away, cut up and diminished, when have I raised my voice? Whom have I tried to persuade or stir into action? In this sacred time, I find myself guilty of idleness, living in an age when falsehoods suffocate thought and language twists logic into writhing, strangling serpents. I stand here before the opening gates, the blaze bright in my eyes, and as I draw near to the force that will judge me, I pass judgment on myself. Put small instruments of destruction in my hands. Let my words become sparks.
outputs.L3:
On the birthday of the world, the speaker pauses to take account of their life. They look honestly at what they have done and at what they have left undone, measuring not only their achievements but also their silences, hesitations, and failures. This moment of reflection becomes a kind of moral inventory, a chance to ask whether their actions have matched their values.

This year, the speaker’s attention turns away from private wounds and personal healing. Instead, they feel called to consider a larger responsibility: the obligation to work for peace. The focus is no longer only on becoming whole as an individual, but on helping to repair a fractured world. Peace is presented not as a vague hope, but as a task that requires courage, commitment, and action.

The speaker then questions the depth of their own courage. They ask how much they have truly risked in the struggle against injustice. Have they defended freedom only when it was safe and convenient, or have they stood firm when doing so carried real consequences? Their concern extends beyond their own liberty to the freedom of others, especially those who are threatened, silenced, or oppressed.

In this reflection, the speaker also condemns their own inaction. They recognize that they have lived in a time marked by lies, manipulation, and attacks on reason, yet they have not always responded with the urgency such a moment demands. Their self-criticism is sharp: silence, they suggest, can become a form of complicity when falsehood and injustice are allowed to grow unchecked.

Finally, the speaker turns toward language itself, asking that their words become more than expressions of regret or intention. They ask for their words to be transformed into instruments of resistance, truth, and change. Rather than remaining passive or ornamental, speech must become active: a force capable of challenging oppression, awakening conscience, and helping to build a more just and peaceful world.
outputs.L4:
In this holy and symbolic season, I find myself drawn inward, as if the calendar itself has become a mirror. It asks me to look closely at what I have done, what I have failed to do, and what still remains broken within me. At first, the work seems personal: to repair what is damaged in my own life, to mend relationships, to correct habits of thought and speech, to become more patient, more honest, more generous. These are necessary tasks, and I do not dismiss them. A person who cannot examine the self honestly will struggle to examine the world honestly.

But the longer I sit with this season of reckoning, the less private it becomes. The questions widen. It is not enough to ask whether I have been kind in small ways, or whether I have kept faith with those nearest to me. I must also ask what I have done in the face of cruelty, violence, oppression, and deceit. Have I worked for peace, or merely wished for it? Have I defended freedom, or only praised it when it cost me nothing? Have I resisted lies, or quietly allowed them to spread because opposition felt inconvenient, frightening, or futile?

This is where my conscience grows heavy. I know that I have too often been passive. I have watched suffering from a distance and called my sorrow compassion. I have recognized injustice and mistaken recognition for action. I have heard falsehoods repeated loudly and, at times, answered them only with silence. Perhaps I told myself that silence was prudence, or humility, or exhaustion. Perhaps I believed that my words were too small to matter. Yet beneath these excuses lies a more painful truth: I did not always want to pay the price of speaking.

The season therefore becomes not only a time of reflection, but a summons. It asks for repentance in the fullest sense—not shame for its own sake, but a turning. A turning away from indifference. A turning away from the comfort of neutrality when neutrality serves the oppressor. A turning away from the easy belief that good intentions are enough. If peace is to be more than a beautiful word, it must be pursued. If freedom is to be more than an inheritance, it must be defended. If truth is to survive, lies must be named.

I do not imagine that words alone can heal the world. Words can be cheap, decorative, even dangerous when they conceal action instead of inspiring it. But words can also be tools. They can cut through deception, open a space for courage, comfort the abandoned, and call the hesitant into motion. A word spoken at the right moment may be a seed, a spark, a hand extended in the dark. It may not be enough, but it is not nothing.

So I begin there, with what I have. I begin with speech that refuses to flatter power. I begin with questions that disturb complacency. I begin with testimony, with memory, with naming what must not be hidden. My words are small, but they are mine to use. And if I have been guilty of passivity, then let my answer now be movement—however modest, however imperfect—toward peace, toward freedom, toward truth, and toward the difficult hope that even small acts of resistance can help change the world.
outputs.L5:
**How, For, Who**

Every meaningful action begins with three simple questions: **How? For whom? Who will benefit?** These questions help us understand purpose, direction, and responsibility.

**How** asks about the method. It encourages us to think carefully, plan wisely, and choose the best way to reach a goal. Whether we are solving a problem, learning a skill, or building something new, “how” guides the process.

**For** reminds us of purpose. We do not act without reason; we act for improvement, for growth, for others, or for a better future. This word connects our efforts to a meaningful goal.

**Who** focuses on people. It asks us to consider the individuals affected by our choices. Who needs help? Who will use the result? Who should be included? By asking “who,” we make our actions more human and thoughtful.

Together, **how, for, and who** create a simple but powerful framework. They help us act with clarity, intention, and care.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical first-person meditation for Rosh Hashanah, using “the birthday of the world” as the opening image, focused on self-judgment, political responsibility, peace, freedom, and the power of words.
counterfactuals.output:
On the birthday of the world, I stand again at the beginning.

The shofar calls me out of sleep—not only the sleep of night, but the heavier sleep of habit, of excuse, of looking away. Its broken cry enters the chambers I keep locked. It asks me what I have done with the breath given to me. It asks what I have built, what I have broken, whom I have harmed, whom I have helped, and whom I have failed to see.

Today I am both witness and defendant. I place my own heart on the scales. I do not come to accuse myself into despair, nor to acquit myself too quickly. I come to tell the truth. I have been generous and I have been afraid. I have spoken up and I have stayed silent. I have longed for justice and still benefited from injustice. I have prayed for peace and carried anger like a private weapon. I have wanted freedom for all, and yet I have guarded my comforts as if they were innocent.

On this day, the world is born again—and so is my responsibility to it.

Let me not imagine that repentance is only inward. The soul is not sealed off from the street, the border, the prison, the voting booth, the marketplace, the school, the hospital, the land beneath our feet. My choices ripple outward. My indifference has consequences. My fear becomes policy when I surrender my voice. My cynicism becomes permission when I call cruelty inevitable.

May I learn to judge myself not only by what I believe, but by what I protect. Not only by what I condemn, but by what I change. Not only by the purity of my intentions, but by the lives touched by my actions.

Ribbono shel Olam, Source of life, teach me a politics of trembling and courage: trembling before the dignity of every person, courage before the powers that deny it. Let me not worship strength when it tramples the vulnerable. Let me not confuse security with domination, or peace with silence, or order with justice. Let me be loyal not to party, tribe, or pride, but to the image of God wherever it appears—especially where I have been taught not to look.

On the birthday of the world, I pray for peace.

Not the thin peace of exhaustion, not the peace of the clenched fist hidden behind the back, not the peace that asks the wounded to be quiet. I pray for a peace with roots: bread, shelter, memory, forgiveness, accountability, land enough to stand on, sky enough to breathe beneath. I pray for the courage to mourn every child, every family, every shattered home, without measuring grief by nationality or creed. I pray for leaders whose hearts can still break. I pray for enemies to become human to one another before more graves are dug.

And I pray for freedom.

Freedom from Pharaoh in every age: from tyranny, hatred, hunger, humiliation, and fear. Freedom from the inner Pharaoh too—the voice that says nothing can change, that my small life does not matter, that cruelty is wisdom, that despair is sophistication. Let me be liberated from the narrow place of my own defensiveness. Let me cross whatever sea must be crossed: from apathy to action, from resentment to repair, from isolation to covenant.

Today, I remember that the world was spoken into being.

“Let there be light”—and light became possible. Words began creation; words continue it. With words we bless and with words we wound. With words we make promises, pass laws, tell histories, erase histories, ask forgiveness, refuse forgiveness, summon mobs, comfort mourners, teach children what is sacred. My mouth is not small. My speech is not nothing. Every day I help create the world with what I say and what I repeat and what I refuse to say.

So let my words be weighed with my deeds.

May I speak truth without cruelty, and kindness without lies. May I resist the language that turns people into objects, enemies into animals, suffering into abstraction. May I not spread what I have not examined. May I not use prayer as a substitute for repair. May the words “I am sorry” become real in my body. May the words “never again” become more than memory. May the words “next year” become a vow.

On the birthday of the world, I begin again.

I do not know what will be written, and I do not know what will be sealed. But I know this: my life is still being asked of me. My hands can still open. My voice can still rise. My heart can still turn. The world, old and aching, is also newborn beneath the horn’s cry.

May I meet it with honesty.

May I meet it with mercy.

May I meet it ready to be changed, and ready to help change what must no longer remain as it is.

Shanah tovah. May this year be sweeter because we have made it more just.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem in the voice of an activist reflecting during the High Holy Days on what they have failed to do for justice and peace; make it fiery, introspective, and morally urgent.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk the shofar enters me like a wound that has learned to sing.

I stand among the living with my fist unclenched, at last, and I am afraid of what it has held back. All year I named the tyrant, named the border, named the burning river and the children coughing under the ash of empires. I marched beneath banners bright as prophecy. I wrote the letters, signed the petitions, raised my voice until my throat tasted of iron. And still—still I made a shelter of my weariness. Still I mistook being right for being righteous. Still I let the hour pass because the meeting was late, because the rain was hard, because despair had a familiar chair waiting for me by the window.

Avinu Malkeinu, I have sinned by saying someday.

I have sinned by scrolling past the face that begged me not to look away. I have sinned by loving peace more than the people who have no peace. I have sinned by wanting justice to arrive clean, without anger, without broken glass, without the terrible inconvenience of the truth knocking at my door after midnight. I have sinned by asking the wounded to be patient while I gathered my courage like loose change from the floor.

The Book opens. Not in heaven only. It opens in the detention cell, in the flooded kitchen, in the school where the heat does not work, in the hospital corridor, in the mouth of the mother naming her dead. Who shall live and who shall die is not a prayer to be recited only—it is a budget, a checkpoint, a vote, a silence. It is the hand I did not extend. It is the risk I did not take.

Let the fast strip me of excuses. Let hunger teach me the shape of another’s constant day. Let my tongue, dry and humbled, remember every word it sharpened for vanity and every word it swallowed from fear. I beat my chest not to perform sorrow, but to wake the sleeping animal there: the heart, stubborn, red, still capable of rebellion.

This year I will not confuse remorse with repair. I will not call myself innocent because I was not holding the weapon. I will not wait for the perfect movement, the flawless leader, the uncomplicated grief. I will go where the cry is loudest. I will bring my body, my money, my name, my Sabbath restlessness, my holy impatience. I will stand between the boot and the breathing. I will be less pure and more useful.

Seal us, if we are to be sealed, in the book of those who rise. Seal us in the book of bread shared, prisons emptied, swords melted down into door hinges for houses that welcome the stranger. Seal us in the book of trees replanted, wages paid, lies interrupted, enemies seen at last as human and therefore no longer easy to kill.

And if the gates are closing, let me run toward them with my hands full of unfinished mercy, shouting: Not yet. Not while one child is cold. Not while one bomb is blessed. Not while one neighbor is made invisible.

The shofar cries again—no, not cries: commands.

Begin.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short literary passage that begins with someone contemplating what they have done and left undone, then shifts into a call for courage against lies, oppression, and war.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk, Mara sat by the cold window and counted what she had done and left undone: the letter never sent, the apology swallowed, the hand she had not reached for when reaching might have mattered. The day seemed to gather these omissions like shadows in the corners of the room.

But beyond the glass, the streets were filling with voices.

She rose, not because she was unafraid, but because fear had been made too useful to tyrants. Let every lie meet a witness. Let every chain hear the hammer of many hands. Let every drum of war be answered by the louder march of the living, who refuse to be fed to hatred. Courage, she thought, is not a fire we wait to feel—it is the small, stubborn light we carry into the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic monologue about standing before divine judgment during a holy season, confessing complacency in a violent political age and asking for language to become a weapon for change.
counterfactuals.output:
I stand here in the season of candles,  
when the dark is taught to open its hands,  
when bells rehearse the trembling names of mercy,  
and the air smells of pine, incense, frost, and ash.

I stand before You—  
not as one falsely accused,  
not as one dragged in chains by history,  
but as one who walked here willingly at last,  
carrying the evidence in my own mouth.

Lord of the threshing floor,  
Judge whose gaze is fire and water,  
look on me.

I have lived in an age of sirens  
and called it weather.  
I have watched the strong grind the weak into headlines  
and learned to lower my eyes  
with the discipline of the comfortable.  
I have mistaken exhaustion for innocence,  
caution for wisdom,  
silence for peace.

Around me, the world has sharpened itself—  
border, bullet, prison, famine, flag—  
and I have polished small phrases  
to keep my conscience warm.  
I have said, “It is complicated,”  
when I meant, “It is costly.”  
I have said, “Someone should speak,”  
when my own tongue lay sleeping  
like an unused blade.

Holy One,  
if there is a book where all things are written,  
write this too:  
I was not always cruel,  
but I was often convenient.  
I did not build every machine of harm,  
but I enjoyed the roads it paved.  
I did not light every fire,  
but I warmed my hands  
and asked no questions of the smoke.

Now the season turns its ancient face toward me.  
The child is expected.  
The lamp is lit.  
The door is marked with longing.  
Angels bend low over the ruined fields  
and sing of peace  
as if peace were not a lullaby,  
but a verdict,  
a summons,  
a hammer striking the locked gate of the world.

So judge me,  
but do not leave me unchanged.

Take this timid language from me—  
these soft evasions,  
these velvet lies,  
these prayers that end  
before they reach the street.

Give me speech with bone in it.  
Give me words that do not flatter power.  
Give me a tongue unafraid of naming the wound,  
and breath enough to keep naming it  
until the wound is seen,  
until the wound is tended,  
until the hand that made it  
is stayed.

Let my language become more than ornament,  
more than smoke rising prettily in sanctuaries.  
Make it a plowshare when the earth must be opened,  
a torch when the house is burning,  
a shelter when the hunted come running,  
a trumpet when the people forget  
they were born for freedom.

And if it must be a weapon,  
let it be so without hatred:  
not a weapon for vanity,  
not a weapon for applause,  
not a weapon that makes another human less human,  
but a weapon against the lie,  
against the numbness,  
against the empire inside my own ribs.

Let every sentence I speak  
be weighed against the hungry child,  
the grieving mother,  
the prisoner counting footsteps,  
the city under thunder,  
the neighbor I have not loved  
because love would interrupt me.

In this holy season,  
do not let me adore innocence  
while abandoning the innocent.  
Do not let me kneel before a cradle  
and rise indifferent to the cross  
being built in the public square.

If I sing,  
make my song accountable.  
If I pray,  
make my prayer combustible.  
If I write,  
let the ink refuse complicity.  
If I am afraid,  
let fear become the door  
through which courage enters.

Judge me, O Mercy.  
Burn away the careful cowardice.  
Leave only what can serve.

Then send me back  
into the violent century  
with a mouth full of dawn,  
with hands ready for repair,  
with words honed bright enough  
to cut a path  
where the silenced may walk through  
singing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a reflective, high-intensity paragraph in the style of a contemporary Jewish feminist poet, mixing personal repentance, political resistance, and images of gates, fire, freedom, and sparks.
counterfactuals.output: At the gate of my own mouth I stand barefoot, ash on my tongue, naming what I have done and what I have allowed to be done in my name; I strike my chest and hear not guilt but a locked city, hear mothers keening, hear children learning the alphabet of smoke, and still the sparks rise, stubborn as prayer. Let my repentance be more than saltwater, more than a bowed head in the old room of mercy: let it be my body in the street, my voice split open against Pharaohs in every uniform, my hands unlearning the empire they were taught to bless. I have carried fear like a mezuzah over the door of my ribs, but tonight I touch it and enter burning—through the narrow gate, through the fire that does not consume, toward a freedom large enough for every exile, every beloved stranger, every name erased and returning in flame.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
